title: Jupiter’s Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth, and it has been shrinking

cover.alt: Black-and-white Voyager 1 image of Jupiter, a striped globe with the oval of the Great Red Spot in its southern half.

body: The Great Red Spot is a giant storm about 22 degrees south of Jupiter’s equator, a high-pressure system whose clouds turn anticlockwise roughly once every 4.5 Earth days, with winds of up to about 430 km/h around its edge. It has been watched continuously since 1878, and it may be older still. But it is getting smaller: at its biggest, more than a century ago, it reached about **40,000 km** across, roughly three Earths, while in 2017 it measured about **16,350 km**, still 1.3 times the width of Earth. Its cloud tops rise about 8 km above the clouds around it.

slides.alt: Black-and-white time-lapse of Jupiter growing larger as a spacecraft approaches: the planet’s light and dark bands slide past one another, and the oval Great Red Spot swirls in the lower half. A few frames are cut off on one side where image data is missing.
slides.caption: Voyager 1’s ‘Blue Movie’, Jan–Feb 1979: 66 images, one every Jupiter rotation of about 10 hours, as the probe closed from 58 to 31 million km. Bands slide past each other around the Great Red Spot.
slides.credit: NASA/JPL · Public domain · shown at 5 frames a second

slides.heading: The Great Red Spot, then and now
slides.note: Width of the oval; its biggest size, over a century ago, is approximate

slides.question: At the edge of the Great Red Spot, how fast do the winds blow, in km/h?
slides.explanation: About 430 km/h (268 mph). The storm turns anticlockwise roughly once every 4.5 Earth days.

slides.heading: Seen up close
slides.text: In 1979 Voyager 1 sent back the first detailed picture of the spot, taken from about 9.2 million km away and showing clouds as small as 160 km across.

slides.question: How long have astronomers watched the Great Red Spot without a break?
slides.explanation: It was first recorded in 1831 and has been watched continuously since about 1878. A spot seen from 1665 to 1713 may or may not have been the same storm.
